Health Care in Crisis

By: Mart-Marie Faure | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Health Ombudsman says Health Care is in crisis, Minister Motsoaledi says its only distressed but doctors on the ground say hospitals have become a death trap.

Unique Selling Point:
Health Ombudsman Professor Makgoba recently stated that the Public Health Care System is in crisis. In a report tabled in parliament in June, the Office of the Health Standards Compliance told the parliamentary committee that only 5 of the 696 hospitals and clinics inspected passed the 80% criteria. 696 Hospitals is only a fifth of the 3 816 public health care facilities in South Africa. Bad management and negative attitude of staff is stated as part of the problem.

Summary:
South Africa's Public Health System is a country wide network of care facilities ranging from mobile and rural clinics to large academic hospitals in urban areas. The public sector is hugely under resourced. Bad management by provinces and corruption play a big role .While the state contributes about 40% of all expenditure on health, the public sector is under pressure to deliver services to about 80% of a growing population. The situation is compounded by health challenges such as HIV and TB and a shortage of medical personnel. Researching and interviewing the situation on the ground, we have uncovered some horror stories told by patients and doctors in public hospitals. Patients dying of septicemia, not being fed properly, patients booked for theater cancelled because theater nurses have exhausted their overtime.

Press Release:


State Hospital Crisis
The Health Ombudsman says the Public Healthcare System is “in crisis”, the Minister of Health says it’s only “distressed” but doctors on the ground say the situation is so dire that State hospitals are becoming death traps. As healthcare workers at provincial hospitals in Mpumalanga struggle to fulfil their daily duties, patients referred for specialist care at Gauteng’s hospitals suffer distress, neglect and treatment delays due to a lack of equipment. Amid dilapidated infrastructure, a lack of management, rampant corruption and administrative overspending, Carte Blanche investigates the real state of public healthcare.


Script:


HEALTH CRISIS SCRIPT

V/O: Macfarlane

Thanda Dlamini was on his way to work in the early hours of the morning when the taxi that he was travelling in was involved in a serious accident. He was brought to Helen Joseph Hospital in Johannesburg.

Nomuza Ndlovu

The call came in at 05h20 in the morning. I left the house at about 06h20.

V/O Macfarlane His wife Nomuza, arrived at the hospital at about 7

Nomuza Ndlovu

They all had dust all over their faces/heads. Dust everywhere.

V/O Macfarlane His gurney was wheeled into a corridor and there he lay...

Nomuza Ndlovu

Wife He said he's feeling cold. I then took off the scarf I was wearing and put it over his body. The door next to him was open, and a cold breeze was coming in. And so we waited, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12...

V/O Macfarlane

Clock: 22:00 At about half past 10, a doctor helped to make the neck brace a bit more comfortable. And after waiting in the passage for an entire day, Thanda was finally taken for a scan late that afternoon. Nomuza had to wheel the gurney herself.

Nomuza Ndlovu

So before they could help they were waiting for the results from a scan. He was left waiting for those results which only came after 12h00, after midnight… I said to him this is how people die in hospitals.

Macfarlane Link What you have just witnessed happens to thousands of patients on a daily basis. Understaffed and

overcrowded hospitals leave seriously ill and injured unattended for hours.

V/O Macfarlane Although Thanda was not attended to for hours, he at least made it to the hospital. Johannes Dlamini and Thembi Mayisela’ s daughter wasn’t that fortunate...

Johannes/ Thembi [00:01:54]Dit was by die oggend. Toe as hulle bel vir my hulle sê nee die kind hy’s siek. Ek kan nie asem uit kry nie. Hulle sê hulle het die ambulanse geroep van 5 uur af se kant.

V/O Macfarlane

More than four hours later the ambulance arrived at their home in Botleng near Delmas.

Thembi Mayisela [00:06:00] THEMBE: He was already dead that time. She was already dead that time.[00:06:30] THEMBE: They just put something like a plaster here and then they just check her then they say no she’s dead.. They are just useless. I think if it wasn’t for the… for the ambulance my daughter she would… she would still alive.

Macfarlane Link .The South African Constitution gives all citizens the right to access healthcare. But, rampant corruption, bad management and a negative work force has the health care system on the verge of collapse.

V/O:Macfarlane

Graphic In June the Office of Health Standards Compliance tabled a damning report in Parliament about the state of public hospitals and clinics. Only five of the 696 hospitals and clinics it inspected in 2016-17 complied with the Department of Health’s standards.. But the inspection covered only a fifth of SA’s 3,816 public health facilities.

V/O: MacFarlane So, what about the remaining three thousand

one hundred and twenty healthcare facilities not inspected? We went and took a first hand look at the extent of the problems in some of the hospitals

V/O: MacFarlane The Tembisa hospital Gauteng serves a population of 2.5 million people. It has 840 beds but is so overcrowded that some patients have to sleep on the ground.

The Mapulaneng Hospital in Bushbuckridge is dilapidated , understaffed and under equipped. Due to a leaking asbestos roof the only operating theatre in the hospital has been closed for almost five months and no operations can be performed..

The Elim, Donald Fraser and Thshilidzini hospitals in Limpopo are all overcrowded, dirty and understaffed.

The Kopanong Hospital in Vereeniging Gauteng has had no hot water in the wards for 9 months. The hospital is in a serious state of disrepair , broken windows are boarded up and the bathrooms in the women’s psychiatric ward are in a shocking state.

And at the back of the Witbank hospital in Mpumalanga we found an ambulance graveyard.

Macfarlane Question Dr Motsoaledi, l think let’s… let’s start right at the beginning and this is the issue of the healthcare system. The Health Ombudsman, the Medical Ombudsman, everyone is coming out and saying it’s on the verge of collapse.

Minister Motsoaledi [00:00:30]It is true that the healthcare system is severely distressed. It’s under severe distress because it’s battling under a huge… you know a high burden of diseases, but also by the population, but also a huge shortage of staff. So we did accept the fact that there are huge, huge problems.For instance, when you look at North West, there was collapse in quite a number hospitals because they were closed. You couldn’t even go there. In other

words you couldn’t even get in and get services, even if you are sick, even if you are about to die, you couldn’t. And that we characterise as a collapse.

Bruce Malumane .[00:00:36 what is happening now is that the minister is presiding over a magnitude of unnecessary deaths of patients.

V/O Macfarlane Dr Bruce Malumane is the Chairperson of the South African Medical Association, Lowveld Branch. He is an outspoken critic of the healthcare system despite being previously suspended for speaking out publicly.

Bruce Malumane

Clinical Manager,

Mapulaneng Hospital The theme tends to be the same in all the provinces where our patients in public sector are not getting the healthcare that they deserve and are entitled.

“Dr M” 00:02:48] DR M: Our hospitals, to be honest, have become a death-trap for the patients. We might have looked at Life Esedimeni as the greatest tragedy but I’m of the view that a greater massacre, bigger than Esedimeni is taking place in our public hospitals

Link MacFarlane Afraid of being suspended , Dr M preferred to keep his identity hidden

“Dr M” [00:12:53 So those are some of the things you… the emotions that the doctors go through. You know, if you’re a paediatrician and you, at some point, is supposed to, you know, choose between which patients… which child to put on C-Pep, which one to remove from the C-Pep, then it’s like you are playing God in a way. And, you know, when you make those decisions, after making that decision, how would you go back home and leave as if nothing has happened.[00:12:53 There are a lot of things that doctors are forced to do and nurses that are not correct to in a way, to cover up for the incompetence of the officials. Because some of the things that you… you sign the oath for, the… you cannot be able to do.

Dr Sifiso Nxumalo [00:00:46]The situation is really troublesome. It

Secretary, SAMA Lowveld Branch needs an urgent intervention, otherwise we’re going to lose more lives than… than we are already losing at the moment.

V/O Macfarlane Dr Sifiso Nxumalo paints a grim picture of the lack of services in the Mapulaneng hospital in Bushbuckridge

Dr Sifiso Nxumalo

Secretary, SAMA Lowveld

Branch We don’t have patient transport in the hospital. We don’t have specialist in the hospital. We don’t have enough clads in the hospital. We don’t have food, which is an essential need. No response will come from the management. They’ll organise a meeting, sit with us. We know your problems, we’re working on them, we’ll give you an answer within a week’s time. Yet, the patients continue to suffer.

V/O Macfarlane But it’s not only in the Mapumaleng hospital where patients are suffering. Sixty two year old Djadji Stam travelled all the way to Johannesburg to tell us her story.

Djaji Drake [00:00:14] It’s been thirteen months of hell.I was diagnosed with gallstones. Being a Sassa grant holder I couldn’t afford private help and I came back to Midrand where I was living at the time and went to register at the Helen Joseph Hospital.

V/O Macfarlane This is where Djadji’s nightmare began.

Djaji Drake 00:13:12 You get spoken to as though you’re a dog and the nursing staff couldn’t care about you. I had a drip in my hand here and was hit on it like that and told there’s no pain, suck it up, you’re tougher than that..

Macfarlane Question [00:07:50]Dr Motsoaledi, you yourself has spoken about a negative workforce, low morale, you know. Some patients have even gone as far as to say that how they’re treated at your hospitals borders on abuse.

Minister Motsoaledi [00:10:25]That the attitude of staff to patient in 80%

of the case is not good. If it’s done by a doctor, you can report that doctor to the Health Professions Council. If it’s done by a nurse, you can report that nurse to the Nursing Council.

V/O Macfarlane But for many patients reporting the abuse and neglect seems futile

Tembi [00:14:51] They don’t care. They don’t care about the people. The only thing they… they care about is to look good and get paid. That’s all.

V/O Macfarlane Even with 200 officials deployed to try and fix a very broken system, to many patients, the departments aim provide a quality, efficient and sustainable health care service for all South Africans just seems to be, a mere pipe dream.

Djaji Drake Quite frankly, the thought of going back into a hospital right now, I’d rather die

PROMO 15” The Public Health Care System is in crisis and on the verge of collapse. Doctors say the situation is so dire that state hospitals are becoming death traps : DR M UPSOUND A greater massacre, bigger than Esedimeni is taking place in our public hospitals

PROMO 15”

Overcrowded hospitals with patients sleeping on the floor, wards without proper sanitation and a negative workforce have become the norm in many of our public health care facilities. DR SIFISO UP SOUND: We don’t have specialist in the hospital. We don’t have enough clerks in the hospital. We don’t have food.
